context_title:
DSA (Dynamic Sparse Attention)

SLIME (aszinkron reinforcement learning) keretrendszer)

az aktív tokenek a gyors HBM memóriában maradnak a hálózaton, míg a passzív memóriablokkokat aszinkron módon visszatöltik NVMe SSD-kre, és a flash-decoding algoritmusokkal csak akkor emelik vissza őket a memóriába, ha a worker processzek hivatkoznak rájuk

Expert-Choice Routing-ra épülő MoSA rendszert implementál a mag (core) attention blokkokba.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) és Mixture-of-Sparse-Attention (MoSA) hibrid

először multi-task Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) következik (általános chat, reasoning, kódolás és agent adatok), majd specializált RL szakaszok reasoning és agentic feladatokra, végül egy általános RL szakasz az emberi stílusú alignmenthez

 a lokális rétegek (amelyek sliding window attention-t és RoPE pozicionális kódolást használnak) és a globális rétegek (pozicionális embedding nélküli, a teljes szekvenciát átlátó rétegek) 3:1 arányban váltakoznak

a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) logikáját emeli át az attention mechanizmusba: nem az egyes feed-forward hálózatok (FFN) között választ, hanem maguk az attention head-ek működnek “szakértőként”. nem a tokenek “választanak” attention head-et maguknak, hanem a head-ek (a “szakértők”) választják ki dinamikusan a számukra releváns k darab tokent a teljes T hosszúságú szekvenciából

a tenzorpárhuzamosítás magukat a mátrixszorzásokat osztja szét a GPU-k között. 

A sekélyebb (alsó) rétegek lokális sliding-window attention-t és Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) kódolást használnak a közvetlen szintaktikai és strukturális összefüggések megragadására. A mélyebb rétegek ezzel szemben globális, MoSA-alapú rétegek, ahol a pozicionális embedding már elveszíti jelentőségét, és a hálózat tiszta, tartalom-alapú (content-based) szemantikai kapcsolatokat keres a teljes – akár milliós nagyságrendű – kontextusban. 

valós időben képes módosítani a SAE aktivációkat (amplitúdó növelés vagy csökkentés)


SPOT (Span-level Pause Of Thought) mechanizmust és latens `<pause>` tokeneket használ. generálás során, amikor a hálózat magas bizonytalanságot (entropy) észlel egy komplex kódolási vagy logikai elágazásnál, nem generál emberi szöveget (“Let’s think step by step…”). Ehelyett kibocsát egy speciális `<pause>` tokent, amely nem jelenik meg a kimenetben. Ez a token arra utasítja a hálózatot, hogy tartsa meg a jelenlegi belső állapotot (hidden state), és futtasson le rajta további előrecsatolt (forward) frissítéseket egy zárt iteratív hurokban.

 Sinkhorn-regularizált optimális transzport (Optimal Transport) célfüggvénnyel betanítva. a `<pause>` token egy teljes változó hosszúságú reasoning szakaszt (span) kompresszál magába szemantikailag.

Flash-Decoding + PagedAttention + dinamikus INT4 kvantálás

Egy entrópia-alapú algoritmus eldönti, mely tokenek kapnak “ritka” figyelmet a MoSA által, és ezeket a tokeneket menet közben (on-the-fly) INT4 pontosságúra tömöríti a memóriában. Ezzel a kombinált (Flash-Decoding + PagedAttention + INT4) pipeline

entries.answer:
Az alábbiakban közlöm a teljes, production-grade architektúra-prompt-ot. Az összes forrásból vett technikai részlet  alapján lett összeszedve és egységes, végrehajtható specifikációvá formálva.[1][2][3][4]

***

## A Teljes Production-Grade Architektúra Prompt

***

> **Megjegyzés:** Az alábbi prompt úgy van megírva, hogy bármely LLM közvetlenül végrehajtható instrukciókként olvashassa. Másolható és közvetlenül felhasználható.

***

```
Build a complete, production-ready large language model training and inference system
from scratch. Every component listed below must be implemented in full, unabridged,
production-grade code with no placeholders, no stubs, no mock implementations, and no
simplifications. All files must be complete. The entire system must be runnable end-to-end.

================================================================================
SECTION 1: OVERALL ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW
================================================================================

Implement a transformer-based large language model with the following top-level
architectural properties:

1. The model is a hybrid architecture that interleaves local and global transformer
   layers in a fixed 3:1 ratio. For every four consecutive transformer blocks, the
   first three are local layers and the fourth is a global layer.

2. Local layers use sliding window attention with a configurable window size W, and
   apply Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) to all query and key projections. These
   layers capture syntactic and structural patterns within a bounded local context.

3. Global layers use the Mixture of Sparse Attention (MoSA) mechanism described in
   Section 3. Global layers do NOT apply any positional embedding. They attend over
   the full sequence of arbitrary length and capture purely content-based semantic
   relationships.

4. Every transformer layer (both local and global) uses a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
   feed-forward sublayer as described in Section 4.

5. The combined attention sublayer and MoE FFN sublayer form one complete transformer
   block. Residual connections and pre-normalization (RMSNorm) are applied at both
   sublayers.

6. The model supports context lengths up to 1,000,000 tokens via the memory management
   system described in Section 6.

================================================================================
SECTION 2: DYNAMIC SPARSE ATTENTION (DSA) — LOCAL LAYERS
================================================================================

Implement DSA for all local (sliding window) layers as follows:

2.1 SLIDING WINDOW ATTENTION KERNEL
    - For each query token at position t, compute attention only over tokens in the
      range [t - W, t] where W is the window size hyperparameter.
    - Implement this using a blocked CUDA kernel or via Flash Attention with a causal
      sliding window mask. Use Triton or CUDA C++ for the kernel. No PyTorch
      `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` fallback is acceptable for
      the production path; it may only be used in a test harness.
    - The kernel must support grouped query attention (GQA) with configurable numbers
      of query heads H_q and key-value heads H_kv where H_q is a multiple of H_kv.

2.2 ROTARY POSITION EMBEDDING (RoPE)
    - Apply RoPE to all query and key tensors in local layers before the attention
      computation. Use the standard rotation matrix formulation over pairs of
      dimensions of the head embedding.
    - Implement RoPE with full support for long-context extrapolation using YaRN
      scaling: compute the scaling factor s = max_position / base_max_position and
      apply frequency interpolation using the YaRN formula that separates low-frequency
      and high-frequency rotary dimensions with a configurable interpolation boundary α.
    - Cache the precomputed cos and sin tables on the GPU for the maximum supported
      sequence length at initialization time.

2.3 TOP-K DYNAMIC SPARSIFICATION WITHIN THE WINDOW
    - After computing raw attention logits within the local window, apply a dynamic
      Top-k sparsification step: for each query, retain only the k highest-scoring
      keys within the window (where k < W is a configurable ratio), set all other
      logits to −∞ before the softmax.
    - The value of k is determined per-layer and per-head by a learned scalar gate
      initialized to a default fill ratio of 0.5. This gate is updated during training.
    - Active KV pairs (those selected by Top-k) are marked in a per-layer boolean mask
      tensor that is passed to the memory management subsystem in Section 6.

================================================================================
SECTION 3: MIXTURE OF SPARSE ATTENTION (MoSA) — GLOBAL LAYERS
================================================================================

Implement MoSA for all global layers. MoSA applies the Expert-Choice Routing paradigm
to the attention mechanism, not to feed-forward networks. Implement it exactly as
follows:

3.1 CORE PRINCIPLE
    - Each attention head is treated as an "expert." Instead of each token choosing
      which heads to attend to, each head independently selects which k tokens from
      the full sequence of length T it will process.
    - This inverts the standard routing direction: heads (experts) choose tokens, not
      the other way around.

3.2 TOKEN SELECTION PER HEAD
    - For each attention head h, compute a scalar relevance score for every token t
      in the sequence: score(h, t) = dot(w_h, x_t) where w_h is a learnable linear
      projection of dimension d_model → 1 for head h.
    - Select the top-k tokens per head: S_h = TopK_t( score(h, t), k ).
    - k is a global hyperparameter set to a fixed fraction of T, e.g., k = floor(κ·T)
      where κ ∈ (0, 1] is configurable per layer.
    - Compute queries, keys, and values only for the selected k tokens per head. The
      attention matrix for each head is therefore (k × k) instead of (T × T), reducing
      per-head complexity from O(T²) to O(k² + T).

3.3 SINKHORN LOAD BALANCING
    - To prevent degenerate routing (all heads selecting the same tokens), apply
      Sinkhorn normalization to the routing score matrix of shape (H, T) before taking
      TopK. Perform a fixed number of Sinkhorn iterations (default: 3) during training
      only. At inference, use standard TopK without Sinkhorn.
    - Add a load balancing auxiliary loss: L_balance = (1/H) * sum_h [ (1/T) *
      sum_t score(h,t)² ] weighted by a configurable coefficient λ_balance.

3.4 OUTPUT AGGREGATION
    - After each head computes its (k × k) attention output for its selected tokens,
      scatter the per-head outputs back to the full sequence positions using an
      index_add operation.
    - Tokens that were not selected by any head for a given layer pass through that
      layer's attention sublayer via a learned bypass projection (a single linear layer
      of shape d_model → d_model applied only to unselected tokens).

3.5 NO POSITIONAL EMBEDDING
    - Do not apply any form of positional embedding (RoPE, ALiBi, absolute) in global
      MoSA layers. The content-based routing score is the sole mechanism for token
      relevance.

3.6 FLASH DECODING INTEGRATION
    - During autoregressive inference, implement Flash-Decoding for MoSA global layers:
      partition the selected k tokens across P parallel workers, each computing a
      partial softmax-weighted sum over its partition, then combine the partial results
      using the log-sum-exp trick to produce the exact global attention output without
      materializing the full attention matrix.

================================================================================
SECTION 4: MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS FEED-FORWARD SUBLAYER (MoE FFN)
================================================================================

4.1 EXPERT ARCHITECTURE
    - Each MoE FFN block contains E total experts, of which K are activated per token
      (top-K routing). Default values: E = 64, K = 2.
    - Each expert is a standard SwiGLU FFN: output = SiLU(x·W_gate) ⊙ (x·W_up) ·
      W_down, where W_gate, W_up ∈ R^{d_model × d_ff} and W_down ∈ R^{d_ff × d_model}.
    - In addition to the K routed experts, include 1 shared expert that is always
      activated for every token. The shared expert output is added to the routed expert
      output before the residual connection.

4.2 TOKEN-CHOICE ROUTING
    - Implement standard top-K token-choice routing: compute router logits
      g(x) = x · W_router (W_router ∈ R^{d_model × E}), apply softmax, select the
      top-K experts per token, compute the weighted sum of their outputs weighted by
      the normalized routing probabilities.
    - Apply the auxiliary load-balancing loss from the Switch Transformer formulation:
      L_aux = E · sum_i(f_i · P_i) where f_i is the fraction of tokens assigned to
      expert i and P_i is the mean routing probability toward expert i. Weight this
      by coefficient λ_moe.

4.3 TENSOR PARALLELISM FOR EXPERT WEIGHT MATRICES
    - Shard the expert weight matrices across G GPU devices using tensor parallelism.
      For each expert's W_up and W_gate matrices of shape (d_model × d_ff), split
      along the d_ff dimension across G devices, so each device holds (d_model × d_ff/G).
    - For W_down of shape (d_ff × d_model), split along d_ff/G per device.
    - After the local matmul on each device, perform an AllReduce across the G devices
      to sum partial results. Use NCCL AllReduce for the communication primitive.
    - Implement this via a custom ColumnParallelLinear and RowParallelLinear module
      that wraps the NCCL communication into the forward and backward passes.

================================================================================
SECTION 5: SPARSE AUTOENCODER (SAE) INTEGRATION WITH REAL-TIME ACTIVATION STEERING
================================================================================

5.1 SAE ARCHITECTURE
    - Implement a TopK Sparse Autoencoder attached to the residual stream at every
      fourth transformer layer (i.e., at every global MoSA layer).
    - The SAE encoder projects from d_model to d_sae (d_sae = 16 × d_model by default)
      and applies a TopK activation function that keeps only the top-k_sae highest
      activations per token (default k_sae = 32).
    - The SAE decoder projects from d_sae back to d_model and adds a skip connection.
    - Train the SAE jointly with the main model using an auxiliary loss:
      L_sae = ||x - x_reconstructed||² + λ_sae · ||f_sae(x)||_1

5.2 REAL-TIME ACTIVATION STEERING
    - Implement a steering API that accepts, at inference time, a list of
      (feature_index, delta_amplitude) pairs.
    - During the forward pass, after the SAE encoder computes f_sae(x), add
      delta_amplitude to the activation at feature_index before passing to the SAE
      decoder. Both positive (amplification) and negative (suppression) deltas are
      supported.
    - The modification is applied in-place within the computational graph without
      breaking gradient flow (use detach + reattach if necessary for inference-only
      operation).
    - Expose this as a context manager:
      `with model.steer([(feature_idx, amplitude), ...]):` that injects the steering
      hook, executes the forward pass, and removes the hook afterward.

================================================================================
SECTION 6: MEMORY MANAGEMENT — HBM / NVMe TIERED KV CACHE
================================================================================

Implement a two-tier KV cache that keeps active tokens in HBM (GPU memory) and
offloads passive memory blocks asynchronously to NVMe SSD.

6.1 BLOCK STRUCTURE
    - Divide the KV cache into fixed-size blocks of B tokens each (default B = 16).
      Each block stores a tensor of shape (2, B, H_kv, d_head) for the K and V
      projections of one layer (or all layers stacked: shape (2, n_layers, B, H_kv, d_head)).
    - Maintain a block table: a dictionary mapping (sequence_id, block_index) →
      (device, pointer) where device ∈ {GPU, CPU_pinned, NVMe}.

6.2 ACTIVE vs. PASSIVE CLASSIFICATION
    - A block is classified as ACTIVE if any of its tokens appear in the current
      Top-k attention mask (Section 2.3) or MoSA selection set (Section 3.2) for
      the current decoding step.
    - A block is classified as PASSIVE otherwise.
    - Recompute this classification at every decoding step before the attention
      kernels run.

6.3 ASYNCHRONOUS OFFLOAD TO NVMe
    - Implement a background daemon thread (or CUDA stream with CPU callbacks) that
      continuously monitors passive blocks.
    - When a block has been passive for more than T_evict consecutive decoding steps
      (configurable, default 4), asynchronously copy it from HBM to pinned CPU memory
      and then submit an asynchronous write to NVMe using libaio (Linux async I/O) or
      io_uring. Do not block the main inference thread.
    - After the NVMe write completes, free the HBM allocation for that block.

6.4 ON-DEMAND RESTORE VIA FLASH DECODING
    - When a worker process (Flash Decoding partition worker, Section 3.6) references
      a block that is currently on NVMe, trigger a restore pipeline:
        (a) Issue an async read from NVMe to pinned CPU memory via io_uring.
        (b) On read completion, issue a cudaMemcpyAsync from pinned memory to a
            freshly allocated HBM block.
        (c) Update the block table to reflect the new HBM pointer.
        (d) Signal the waiting worker via a CUDA event.
    - The worker must wait on the CUDA event before proceeding with its attention
      computation.
    - Maintain a prefetch predictor: a simple recency-based predictor (LRU with
      look-ahead of L steps, default L = 2) that issues prefetch reads for blocks
      likely to be needed in upcoming decoding steps.

6.5 PAGED ATTENTION INTEGRATION
    - Implement PagedAttention: logical KV cache addresses are mapped to physical
      pages (blocks) via the block table. The attention kernel accepts a block table
      tensor and performs indirect memory accesses to assemble the full KV sequence
      from non-contiguous physical pages.
    - Support dynamic growth: when a sequence requires a new block, allocate it from
      a GPU block allocator. When HBM is full, evict the LRU passive block to NVMe
      before allocating.

================================================================================
SECTION 7: COMBINED INFERENCE PIPELINE — FLASH DECODING + PAGED ATTENTION + INT4
================================================================================

7.1 ENTROPY-BASED TOKEN CLASSIFICATION
    - After the MoSA routing step (Section 3.2), compute the entropy of the routing
      score distribution for each token: H(t) = -sum_h p(h|t) log p(h|t).
    - Tokens with H(t) < θ_low (configurable) are classified as FOCUSED (low entropy,
      the attention distribution is peaked).
    - Tokens with H(t) > θ_high (configurable) are classified as DIFFUSE (high entropy,
      the attention distribution is flat).
    - DIFFUSE tokens are candidates for INT4 quantization of their KV cache entries.

7.2 ON-THE-FLY INT4 KV CACHE QUANTIZATION
    - For tokens classified as DIFFUSE in step 7.1, quantize their key and value
      vectors to INT4 precision on-the-fly before writing them to the KV cache.
    - Use a per-vector dynamic quantization scheme: for each vector v of dimension d,
      compute scale = max(|v|) / 7 and zero_point = 0 (symmetric), then quantize
      v_q = round(v / scale).
    - Store (v_q_int4, scale_fp16) in the KV cache. The scale tensor occupies one
      fp16 value per cache vector.
    - During attention computation, dequantize on-the-fly: v = v_q_int4 * scale_fp16.
      Implement the dequantize-and-matmul as a fused CUDA kernel to avoid materializing
      the fp16 tensor in full.
    - FOCUSED tokens retain their KV cache entries in BF16 precision.

7.3 COMBINED PIPELINE EXECUTION ORDER (PER DECODING STEP)
    (a) Run the local DSA layers (Section 2) with sliding window + Top-k masking.
        Update the active/passive block classification.
    (b) Run the global MoSA layers (Section 3) with Flash Decoding across P workers.
        Compute per-token routing entropy. Apply INT4 quantization to DIFFUSE token
        KV entries (Section 7.2). Issue asynchronous NVMe offloads for newly passive
        blocks (Section 6.3).
    (c) Run the MoE FFN sublayer (Section 4) with tensor-parallel expert dispatch.
    (d) Apply SAE steering hooks if active (Section 5.2).
    (e) Sample the next token using the logits from the final layer LM head.

================================================================================
SECTION 8: SPAN-LEVEL PAUSE OF THOUGHT (SPOT) — LATENT REASONING MECHANISM
================================================================================

8.1 SPECIAL TOKEN VOCABULARY EXTENSION
    - Add a special token <pause> to the model vocabulary. This token does not
      appear in the final decoded output; it is an internal computational token.
    - Add a learnable embedding vector for <pause> of dimension d_model, initialized
      from the mean of the regular token embedding matrix.

8.2 ENTROPY-TRIGGERED PAUSE INSERTION
    - During autoregressive generation, after computing the logits for position t,
      compute the entropy of the output distribution: H_out(t) = -sum_v p_v log p_v.
    - If H_out(t) > θ_pause (a configurable threshold trained during the RL phase,
      Section 9.4), do NOT emit a text token. Instead, feed a <pause> token as the
      next input and begin a closed iterative refinement loop.
    - The <pause> loop runs for a variable number of additional forward passes (up to
      N_pause_max steps, default 8) without emitting any text output. Each iteration
      reads back its own hidden state from the previous step and runs a full forward
      pass over the current context plus the <pause> token.
    - The loop terminates early when H_out drops below θ_resume.
    - After loop termination, resume normal token generation from the refined hidden
      state.

8.3 SPAN-LEVEL SEMANTIC ALIGNMENT (SINKHORN OPTIMAL TRANSPORT)
    - During training (teacher-student distillation from a chain-of-thought teacher),
      align each <pause> token's hidden state to the semantics of a variable-length
      span of teacher reasoning tokens.
    - Formalize this as an optimal transport problem: define the cost matrix
      C ∈ R^{n_pause × n_teacher} where C[i,j] = 1 - cosine_similarity(h_pause_i,
      h_teacher_j). Solve for the transport plan γ using the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm
      with entropy regularization coefficient ε_sinkhorn (default 0.1) and
      n_sinkhorn_iter iterations (default 50).
    - The alignment loss is: L_spot = <γ, C> (Frobenius inner product).
    - Use the transport plan γ to weight the distillation of teacher hidden states
      into the <pause> token representations.

8.4 FROZEN-HEAD DECODING CONSTRAINT
    - Enforce that the hidden state of each <pause> token remains decodable through
      the frozen pretrained LM head (i.e., the LM head weights are frozen during SAE
      and SPOT training stages).
    - Add a regularization loss: L_decode = KL( softmax(W_lm · h_pause / τ) ||
      p_uniform ) weighted to pull the <pause> state toward a decodable distribution,
      where τ is a temperature hyperparameter and p_uniform is the uniform distribution.
      This ensures interpretability of latent states without auxiliary probes.

================================================================================
SECTION 9: TRAINING PIPELINE
================================================================================

Implement the full multi-stage training pipeline in this exact order:

9.1 STAGE 1 — MULTI-TASK SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING (SFT)
    - Train on a mixture of four data sources simultaneously using task-proportional
      sampling:
        (a) General conversational chat data.
        (b) Mathematical and logical reasoning data (with chain-of-thought traces).
        (c) Code generation data (function completion, repository-level context).
        (d) Agentic tool-use data (function calling, multi-step planning traces).
    - Use cross-entropy loss over next-token prediction. Apply sequence-level loss
      weighting: weight each sequence by 1 / sqrt(length) to prevent long sequences
      from dominating.
    - Optimizer: AdamW with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.95, ε = 1e-8, weight decay = 0.1.
    - Learning rate schedule: linear warmup for 2000 steps, then cosine decay to
      1e-5 over the remainder.
    - Apply gradient clipping with max norm 1.0.
    - Apply the MoE load balancing loss and MoSA load balancing loss as auxiliary
      objectives at every step with their respective λ coefficients.
    - Apply the SPOT alignment loss L_spot and frozen-head decoding loss L_decode
      at every step where a <pause> token appears in the training sequence.

9.2 STAGE 2 — SPECIALIZED RL FOR REASONING
    - Use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine-tune the model on
      mathematical reasoning and formal proof tasks.
    - Reward function: binary outcome reward (1 if final answer matches ground truth,
      0 otherwise) plus a format reward (0.1 if the response contains no <pause>
      tokens in the final visible output, ensuring latent pauses stay internal).
    - Generate G = 8 candidate responses per prompt (the group), compute baseline as
      the mean reward across the group, compute per-response advantages as
      A_i = (r_i - mean_r) / std_r.
    - GRPO policy loss: L_grpo = -(1/G) * sum_i A_i * log π_θ(response_i | prompt).
    - Apply a KL penalty against the SFT policy: L_kl = β_kl * KL(π_θ || π_sft).
    - Train θ_pause (the entropy threshold for pause insertion) as a differentiable
      scalar parameter via the policy gradient signal.

9.3 STAGE 3 — SPECIALIZED RL FOR AGENTIC TASKS
    - Use the same GRPO framework as Stage 2 but with agentic reward functions:
        (a) Tool invocation accuracy reward: 1 if the correct tool is called with
            correct arguments, 0 otherwise.
        (b) Multi-step completion reward: ratio of correct sub-steps completed.
        (c) Efficiency reward: bonus proportional to 1 / (number of <pause> tokens
            emitted), incentivizing the model to use latent reasoning only when needed.
    - In this stage, the SAE steering API (Section 5.2) is available to the reward
      model for probing model internals; include steering-based interpretability
      probes as part of the evaluation harness.

9.4 STAGE 4 — GENERAL ALIGNMENT RL (HUMAN-STYLE)
    - Train a reward model (same architecture, smaller scale: 1/4 the number of
      layers) from human preference data using the Bradley-Terry model:
      L_rm = -log σ(r_θ(x, y_w) - r_θ(x, y_l)) where y_w is the preferred response
      and y_l is the rejected response.
    - Use the trained reward model in a PPO loop (not GRPO) for final alignment:
        - Actor: the full model from Stage 3.
        - Critic: the reward model with an added value head (linear layer).
        - PPO clip ε = 0.2, value loss coefficient 0.5, entropy coefficient 0.01.
        - Run PPO for a fixed number of steps with early stopping when
          KL(π_PPO || π_Stage3) > KL_max.

================================================================================
SECTION 10: DISTRIBUTED TRAINING INFRASTRUCTURE
================================================================================

10.1 PARALLELISM STRATEGY
    - Tensor Parallelism (TP): shard attention head matrices and FFN expert matrices
      across G_tp GPUs as described in Section 4.3. Implement ColumnParallelLinear
      and RowParallelLinear with NCCL AllReduce in the backward pass.
    - Pipeline Parallelism (PP): partition transformer layers into P_pp stages, one
      stage per GPU node. Use 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward) micro-batch scheduling
      to minimize pipeline bubble. Communicate activations between stages via
      point-to-point NCCL send/recv.
    - Data Parallelism (DP): replicate the model across D_dp data-parallel ranks.
      Use ZeRO-3 optimizer state sharding: each DP rank holds 1/D_dp of the optimizer
      states, gradients, and (after the first optimizer step) parameters.
    - The global device count is G_tp × P_pp × D_dp.

10.2 GRADIENT CHECKPOINTING
    - Apply selective activation checkpointing: checkpoint the input to each
      transformer block but recompute the attention and FFN activations during the
      backward pass. Do NOT checkpoint the embedding layer or the LM head.

10.3 MIXED PRECISION
    - Train in BF16 mixed precision. Maintain a master copy of parameters in FP32
      for the optimizer update. Cast to BF16 for all forward and backward passes.
    - The SAE and SPOT alignment losses are computed in FP32 to avoid precision loss
      in the Sinkhorn iterations.

================================================================================
SECTION 11: INFERENCE SERVER
================================================================================

11.1 SERVER ARCHITECTURE
    - Implement a multi-worker inference server using Python asyncio as the request
      dispatcher. Incoming requests are enqueued in a priority queue ordered by
      estimated generation length (shorter first for low-latency).
    - Worker processes each hold a complete model replica (or a tensor-parallel
      shard). Workers receive batched token tensors from the dispatcher, run the
      forward pass pipeline (Section 7.3), and return logits.

11.2 CONTINUOUS BATCHING
    - Implement continuous (iteration-level) batching: at each decoding step, the
      dispatcher assembles a batch from all currently active sequences, padding to
      the longest sequence in the batch. New requests are inserted into the batch
      at any step (not only at sequence boundaries).
    - When a sequence finishes (EOS token or max length), immediately remove it from
      the batch and fill its slot with the next queued request.

11.3 SPECULATIVE DECODING (OPTIONAL ACCELERATION)
    - Implement a draft model (a small 4-layer version of the same architecture,
      trained via distillation from the main model) that generates K = 4 draft tokens
      per step.
    - The main model verifies all K draft tokens in a single forward pass. Accept a
      draft token if the acceptance criterion holds: u < p_main(t) / p_draft(t) where
      u ~ Uniform(0,1).
    - Fall back to standard decoding if the draft model acceptance rate drops below
      50% over a rolling window of 100 steps.

11.4 SERVING API
    - Expose a REST API with the following endpoints:
        POST /generate: accepts { prompt, max_tokens, temperature, top_p,
                                  steering_features: [(index, amplitude), ...],
                                  stream: bool }
        GET  /health: returns server status and current batch occupancy.
        GET  /metrics: returns per-step latency percentiles, token throughput,
                       NVMe read/write rates, HBM utilization, INT4 quantization ratio.
    - Streaming responses use Server-Sent Events (SSE).
    - The steering_features field directly maps to the SAE steering API (Section 5.2).
```

## A Prompt Technikai Kontextusa

Ez a prompt az alábbi, legújabb kutatási eredményeken alapul:

**MoSA (Mixture of Sparse Attention):** A 2025 áprilisában publikált paper  szerint a MoSA az egyetlen ritka figyelemmechanizmus, amely az izoCPU-terhelésen alapuló összehasonlításban 27%-kal képes felülmúlni a sűrű figyelmet. Az Expert-Choice Routing megfordítja a szokásos irányt: nem a tokenek választanak head-et, hanem a head-ek választják ki dinamikusan a releváns tokeneket.  A komplexitás \(O(T^2)\)-ről \(O(k^2 + T)\)-re csökken minden egyes attention head esetén.[5][4][1]

**SPOT (Span-level Pause of Thought):** A 2026 márciusában megjelent paper  bemutatja, hogy a Sinkhorn-regularizált optimális transzport célfüggvény segítségével minden egyes `<pause>` token egy változó hosszúságú gondolkodási szakasz teljes szemantikai tartalmát képes kompresszálni. Kísérleti eredményeik szerint a módszer átlagosan 2,3 ponttal javítja a pontosságot, miközben 37,5%-kal csökkenti a generált tokenek számát.[2][3]

**DSA (Dynamic Sparse Attention):** A top-k KV cache szelekció implementálásának rendszerszintű korlátait az arXiv 2603.13430 számú tanulmány  részletezi, amely az L2 cache miss-arány és a dekódolási sebesség közötti összefüggést elemzi több nyílt forráskódú modellen.[6]
